beats: Burning edges, frozen middle. Your microwave isn't broken.
Its waves simply can't reach the center of your food.
A tube called a magnetron fires microwaves into the metal box.
They flip water molecules back and forth billions of times a second, and that jiggling is heat.
But every layer of food absorbs some energy, so the waves fade as they go, like light sinking into deep water.
After two or three centimetres, about an inch, they're almost gone.
Everything deeper heats the slow way: warmth creeping inward from the hot outer shell.
Frozen food makes it worse: ice barely absorbs microwaves at all.
So the thawed edges grab all the energy and keep getting hotter.
That's why a thin plate heats evenly, and a thick block doesn't: its core sits beyond the waves' reach.
Your microwave doesn't cook from the inside. It cooks the shell, and the shell cooks the rest.
